summary:
Castilla-La Mancha stands under Spain's national framework: Ley 4/2023 of 28 February 2023, published in the Boletín Oficial del Estado, applies uniformly across all autonomous communities, including this one, and the source inventory identifies no facility, expression or assembly restriction enacted at regional level.

Document-relevant provision is national and administrative. Adults may request rectification of the sex entry on their own registry entry directly before the Civil Registry, without prior surgical reassignment, a gender-dysphoria diagnosis or two years of medical treatment; the right is grounded in the free development of personality under Article 10.1 of the Constitution. Recognition is possible from age 12 under conditions, a provision that proved contentious during passage.

Because access to sex-separated facilities rests on the gender marker recorded in the civil registry rather than on biological sex, that registry entry is the operative basis for facility rules in Castilla-La Mancha, in contrast to the stricter single-sex-space approach being adopted in the United Kingdom on biological-sex lines with restrictions applied case by case rather than as a blanket ban.

Ley 4/2023 defines and sanctions discriminatory conduct and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation, sexual identity, gender expression and sexual characteristics, declares discriminatory contract clauses null and void, obliges discrimination data collection broken down by the covered causes, and mandates measures adapted to rural circumstances. The statute also bans non-consensual normalising surgeries on intersex children, expands assisted reproduction rules, provides parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples, strengthens sexuality education, and prohibits discrimination in healthcare, employment and housing. Same-sex marriage and full adoption rights have been in force since 2005, and legal gender change does not require surgery or sterilisation.

There is no free-standing criminal offence of gender-expression-based hate crime: the phrase 'gender expression' appears in no article of the Spanish Criminal Code. The hate-speech aggravating circumstance in Article 22.4 and the penalties of Article 510 (one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months) derive from Organic Law 6/2022, while Ley 4/2023 itself reformed offences against sexual freedom, including Articles 132, 173, 178 to 181 and 189 bis.

Enforcement of the gender-identity aggravation is documented at first-instance level. In July 2026 the Tribunal de Instancia in Vigo applied the transfobia aggravating circumstance for the first time in a misdemeanour case concerning threats sent by WhatsApp to a trans woman, fining the author EUR 300. In a separate case reported on 8 January 2026, a juvenile gang harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park in Valencia to mock them; the only adult defendant received six months' prison and two minors were judged separately.
tangentialFactors:
Comparatively, Spain's administrative self-declaration regime places it alongside Argentina, Ireland, Portugal and Uruguay. A 2016 23-country survey ranked Spain the most trans-supportive of the group surveyed and the only country where a majority supported unrestricted legal gender designation change, a dated baseline predating the 2023 law.

The national Trans Law's passage was contentious, particularly the provision allowing children from age 12 to obtain legal gender recognition under conditions.
localsOnly:
Residents of Castilla-La Mancha benefit from the same national administrative route as all of Spain: rectification of the sex entry on one's own civil registry record is requested directly before the Civil Registry, with no requirement of diagnosis, surgery or a waiting period of medical treatment.

The law obliges public bodies and covered entities to collect discrimination data broken down by the protected causes, including gender identity and gender expression, and to adopt measures adapted to rural circumstances, relevant to the largely rural character of this autonomous community.

Discriminatory contract clauses are null and void, and discriminatory conduct and harassment on grounds of sexual identity, gender expression or sexual characteristics are sanctioned under the national statute.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not resolve whether Castilla-La Mancha has enacted any regional implementing decree, funding programme or regional complaints mechanism under Ley 4/2023; only the national statute's uniform application is sourced.

No source in the inventory addresses waiting times, registry office capacity or practical processing delays for gender-marker rectification in this autonomous community.

The two enforcement examples cited (Vigo and Valencia) fall outside Castilla-La Mancha and are illustrative of national judicial practice rather than regional outcomes; no first-instance transfobia aggravation case from this autonomous community is sourced.

Whether regional healthcare providers in Castilla-La Mancha offer gender-affirming care, and on what waiting lists, is not sourced.
